# Question

**Does watching cat videos improve mood?** Myrick (2015, *Computers in Human Behavior*) surveyed 6,795 respondents about cat-video viewing and rated 11 emotion scales before vs after (retrospective pre/post).

## Data source

Published Table 2 aggregates (means/SDs, published t); the analytic paired t from these moments reproduces the published t within Δ ≈ 0.34.

# Exploratory analysis

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Mean emotion change (after − before) across the 11 scales"
d = df.assign(change=df["mean_after"] - df["mean_prior"]).sort_values("change")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.6))
ax.barh(d["label"], d["change"],
        color=np.where(d["change"] > 0, "#8fbf8f", "#c76c6c"))
ax.axvline(0, color="k", lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Mean change (after − before), 1–5 scale")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

# Methods & results

Analytic paired t-tests from published moments for all 11 scales; for the two composites, per-person paired data simulated (seed 2026) for sign-flip randomization (100k) and bootstrap CIs.

| Composite | Mean change | Paired t | Randomization p | Bootstrap 95% CI |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Positive emotions | +0.77 | t = 51.1 | < 1e-5 | (0.74, 0.80) |
| Negative emotions | −0.74 | t = −60.1 | < 1e-5 | (−0.77, −0.71) |

# Decision

**Mood improves substantially after cat videos** — all 11 emotion scales move favourably (|t| ≥ 26). But this is a within-person retrospective association (recall and mood-congruent biases possible), not a causal experiment.
